instructions.content: Ask exactly ONE question per turn via AskUserQuestion -- never bundle multiple questions into one call even though the tool nominally supports up to four.
Every question offers 3-4 concrete, mutually exclusive options, each with a short description of what picking it implies or its main tradeoff -- never a bare label alone.
The free-text/"Other" path must always remain open, whether via AskUserQuestion's automatic handling or an explicit invitation in plain chat.
Let the previous answer choose the next question -- work adaptively instead of marching through a fixed list irrespective of what was answered.
Stop as soon as you have enough to act; most interviews resolve in 3-6 questions.
Recap every answer in a short bulleted list and get explicit confirmation before finalizing, unless the user has explicitly waived the recap.
Only after confirmation, produce the output -- default to a synthesized chat answer; write a file only when the interview is clearly feeding downstream work the user already asked for.
NEVER ask more than one question per turn, even as a single AskUserQuestion call bundling several -- it forces the user to hold several decisions in mind and breaks the adaptive chain.
NEVER offer fewer than 3 or more than 4 options on a question that has a real decision space -- two options force a false binary, five or more overloads working memory.
NEVER hide or omit the free-text path -- concrete options speed up the common case but the user's actual answer may not be listed.
NEVER keep asking after the user gives a clear "here's my answer, let's move on" or "just decide" signal.
NEVER let the recap silently drop, merge, or reinterpret an answer -- the recap is the user's only checkpoint before the output is produced.
NEVER produce a written file the user did not ask for and that isn't clearly needed by downstream work.
PREFER a direct answer instead of opening the interview when the ask is mechanical or the user is visibly time-constrained.
TYPICALLY the whole interview resolves in 3-6 questions -- treat that as a rough budget, not a hard cap.
